name: Kimashami / Madschamedialekt
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 3 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Augustiny, Julius. 1914. Kurzer Abriß des Madschamedialekts. (Archiv für das Studium deutscher Kolonialsprachen, Bd. XVI.) Berlin: Druck und Kommissionsverlag von Georg Reimer. x+106 pp. Google Books, id PtFHAQAAMAAJ (Univ. of Illinois copy); = HathiTrust osu.32435005818869.
catalog_locator: Vorwort, p. VII, last paragraph before 'Zum Schluß..' / 'Der Verfasser.' (listed as 'Betonung' in the Inhaltsverzeichnis, p. IX); Google Books page-id RA2-PR7 (page scan held); context pp. V-VI (RA2-PR5, RA2-PR6).
catalog_quote: Die genaue Aussprache des Madschamedialekts kann man nicht aus diesem Buche lernen, sondern nur im mündlichen Verkehr mit den Eingebornen. Im allgemeinen werden die Wörter im Kimashami auf der vorletzten, seltener auf der drittletzten Silbe betont. Ist dagegen die letzte Silbe eines Wortes lang, was durch einen Strich über dem Endvokal ausgedrückt ist, dann erhält diese den Ton. [p. VII; the macron convention, p. VII top: ū ist langes, geschlossenes u wie in „Kuh“, z. B. kū „alt“; rū „umsonst“. — and p. VI: ō ist lang und geschlossen wie oo in „Boot“; z. B. kō „jung“. Ist es aber durch Kontraktion von waa entstanden, so ist es lang und offen wie das o im französischen Worte „mort“; z. B. shikabō (aus shikabwaa) „ich werde geschlagen werden“.]
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Machame (mach1266) is not in the catalog. this search of works with stress in the title had one title hit, Philippson's 1991/1992 Paris 5 thesis 'Tons et accent dans les langues bantu d'Afrique orientale' (542 pp., French): a comparative typology/diachrony of ~30 East Bantu prosodic systems from fully tonal to demarcative-penultimate-stress. Only the theses.fr abstract is open (accessible: non; not on HAL, archive.org, or Google Books preview; SUDOC holds the thesis and an ANRT microfiche), and the abstract does not name Chaga/Machame, so relevance stays 'unclear' and it is worth acquiring at medium priority (it would give Philippson's placement of Mashami on the tone-to-accent spectrum, if included). The best first-hand stress statement actually read is Augustiny 1914, Vorwort p. Modern sources held by the project (Yukawa 1989 tonology, Philippson & Montlahuc 2003, Rugemalira 2014) describe Mashami as a tone language and say nothing about word stress. WorldCat and ddl.cnrs.fr were unreachable.

new_statements.quote: Im allgemeinen werden die Wörter im Kimashami auf der vorletzten, seltener auf der drittletzten Silbe betont. Ist dagegen die letzte Silbe eines Wortes lang, was durch einen Strich über dem Endvokal ausgedrückt ist, dann erhält diese den Ton.
new_statements.translation: In general, words in Kimashami are stressed on the penultimate syllable, more rarely on the antepenultimate. If, however, the last syllable of a word is long, which is indicated by a stroke over the final vowel, then that syllable receives the stress.

Ist dagegen die letzte Silbe eines Wortes lang, was durch einen Strich über dem Endvokal ausgedrückt ist, dann erhält diese den Ton.' followed by 'Zum Schluß will ich nur noch bemerken, daß das Zeitwort im Kimashami viel reicher an Formen ist als im Suaheli. Der Verfasser.' The quote in the report is verbatim. Surrounding section read: Vorwort pp. V-VII (PR5, P…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default word stress on the penult; a minority of words have antepenultimate stress; a word-final long vowel (written with a macron, e.g. kū 'alt', shikabō) attracts stress to the final syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: Antepenultimate stress 'more rarely'; final stress when the final syllable is long (macron-marked final vowel, often from contraction, e.g. -bō < -bwaa).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('die Wörter'), citation/orthographic forms in a practical missionary grammar; impressionistic, no tone marking. Modern descriptions (Sharp 1954, Yukawa 1989, Philippson & Montlahuc 2003) analyse Machame as a tone language (H/L with tone shift, super-high surface tones) and make no stress statement, so Augustiny's 'Betonung' may partly reflect perceived pitch prominence.
new_statements.identity_note: Augustiny 1914 describes 'Kimashami', the speech of the Landschaft Madschame (Machame proper, west Kilimanjaro) = Glottolog mach1266 (Machame; cf. dialect masa1296 Masama). Fokken 1905 'Das Kisiha' describes the Siha dialect (Glottolog siha1242, listed under mach1266). Yukawa 1989 and Sharp 1954 are Machame proper. McHugh's Chaga work is KiVunjo (vunj1238), a different languoid.

new_statements.quote: [PDF p.288, ch.4 §7.3.2] Le chaga (de même que des langues voisines, comme le kamba) est une langue où jouent en même temps un système tonal entièrement distinctif et un système d'accent démarcatif, les effets des deux s'entrecroisant. [...] certains nominaux sortent du stade lexical avec une syllabe accentuée (soit la pénultième, soit la finale) [...] [PDF p.483, ch.6 §3.5.2] c) langues à culmination de longueur, mais non de hauteur, sur la pénultième (langues à prosodèmes distinctifs, mais sans opposition de longueur) : [...] asu; daʃida et saghala; chaga; [PDF p.446, ch.6 §2.7.1] Dans le groupe XXI, les quatre schèmes BC se sont bien maintenus. Exemples (gweno et mashami) : [BB Wama 'viande', HB múWi 'manche', BH mmbá 'maison', HH Ngúkú 'poulet']
new_statements.translation: Chaga (like neighbouring languages such as Kamba) is a language in which a fully distinctive tonal system and a demarcative accent system operate at the same time, their effects interweaving. [...] some nominals leave the lexical stratum with an accented syllable (either the penultimate or the final) [...] c) languages with a culmination of length, but not of pitch, on the penultimate (languages with distinctive prosodemes but no length contrast): ... Asu; Dabida and Saghala; Chaga; [...] In group XXI [Chaga] the four Common Bantu tone schemes have been well preserved. Examples (Gweno and Mashami): [LL, HL, LH, HH noun stems].
new_statements.citation: Philippson, Gérard (1991). Tons et Accent dans les Langues Bantu d'Afrique Orientale: Étude Comparative Typologique et Diachronique. Université de Paris V - René Descartes. 542 pp.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's Augustiny 1914 record (general penultimate 'Betonung', final when the last vowel is long): Philippson places Chaga among languages with a demarcative length culmination on the penultimate and, for Vunjo, a lexical accent that is penultimate or, after vowel coalescence (which yields long final vowels), final - the same right-edge pattern Augustiny heard. It adds what Augustiny lacks: Chaga, and Mashami specifically (four preserved Common Bantu tone schemes, pp.446-447), is a tone language, and the 'accent' is demarcative (group-final length) interacting with tone rather than a plain word stress. Caveat: the accent analysis is of the Vunjo (Central Chaga, Glottol…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Chaga as a whole (Philippson's group XXI, which he divides into West Chaga = Mashami/Rwa/Siha, Central = Vunjo/Mochi, East, plus Gweno) is treated as a tone language that keeps the four Common Bantu lexical tone schemes (shown explicitly for Mashami noun stems, pp.446-447) and in addition has a demarcative accent: the penultimate syllable carries a culmination of length (not of pitch), realised only at the end of a prosodic group; in the Central (Vunjo) dialect analysed in detail the lexical accent is 'partially free', normally on the stem penultimate, on the final in monosyllabic stems and in stems with vowel coalescence (ua > o, e.g. passives), and absent in a few ethnonyms, and it interacts with tone to create super-high tones. No Mashami-specific accent/stress rule is stated; the detailed accent analysis is of Vunjo (after McHugh 1990) and the penultimate-length statement is made for 'chaga' generically.
new_statements.exceptions: Vunjo only: stems accented on the final syllable are essentially monosyllabic stems ('tous les thèmes monosyllabiques en chaga portent l'accent sur leur unique syllabe', p.289) or products of vowel coalescence (passives ua>o, p.386); unaccented stems are only ethnonyms derived from place names (p.386, 447); accent distinctions disappear word-internally in a prosodic group since the demarcative accent is realised only group-finally (p.387); an accent-retraction rule H B* -> H* B neutralises penult vs final accent in HL stems (p.390).
new_statements.identity_note: Philippson's Chaga accent data are from the Vunjo (Central Chaga, Kilema/Marangu area; Glottolog vunj1238) dialect after McHugh 1990, plus a Mochi verb example; Mashami (= Machame, Kimashami, Augustiny's 'Madschame', West Chaga E621, mach1266) appears only in the dialect classification (p.73: chaga-ouest = mashami, rwa, siha) and in the diachronic tone-correspondence table (pp.446-447). The generic statements about 'chaga' (tonal + demarcative penultimate length accent) are offered for the group as a whole.

tone_statements.quote: また, タンザニアのチャガ(Chaga)語マチャメ(Machame)方言では, あとに何も続かないか低く平らな名詞が続く時と, あとにどこか高いところがある名詞が続く時で, 動詞活用形のアクセントが異なることが多いが, 奇妙なことには, うしろのほうが変異するのでなく, 前のほうで変異する。^は下降調を示す。 m-bá-lé-lélémba (ndu)「彼らは(人を)なだめた」 m-bá-le-lélémba moonâ「彼らは子供をなだめた」
tone_statements.translation: Also, in the Machame dialect of the Chaga language of Tanzania, the accent [tone pattern] of conjugated verb forms often differs between when nothing follows or a low, flat noun follows, and when a noun that has a high somewhere follows; but strangely, it is not the rear part that varies but the front part. ^ marks a falling tone. m-bá-lé-lélémba (ndu) 'they soothed (a person)'; m-bá-le-lélémba moonâ 'they soothed the child'.

tone_statements.summary: Tonal ('accent' = tone per the intro); one paragraph on Machame: verb-form tone varies with a following noun's tone, H and falling marks; no inventory; syllable-toneme framing p.31 is general Bantu.

readall_conflicts: No outright contradiction. The catalog record (Augustiny 1914) codes Kimashami as penultimate stress, occasionally antepenultimate, final when the final vowel is long (weight-hedged). Philippson 1991, now read from the open author copy, treats Chaga (group XXI, which includes Mashami) as a tone language - Mashami noun stems preserve all four Common Bantu tone schemes - with a superimposed demarcative accent realised as a length culmination on the penultimate of the prosodic group, and (for the Vunjo dialect he analyses) a partially free lexical accent on the penultimate or, via vowel coalescence, the final syllable. This supports the penultimate/final-long part of Augustiny's observation while reframing it as demarcative accent in a tonal system; it gives no support for antepenultimate placement and states nothing specific to Mashami accent, since the detailed analysis is of Vunjo (vunj1238).

sources.quote: Ces systèmes varient en effet depuis des langues pleinement tonales (kikuyu) jusqu'à des langues à accent démarcatif pénultième (swahili), tous les cas intermédiaires étant représentés. [...] Une trentaine de langues en tout sont utilisées comme exemples. Enfin, on établit systématiquement les correspondances prosodiques entre chacune des langues concernées et le bantu commun et on propose l'hypothèse que le moteur principal de l'évolution des systèmes concernés a été l'émergence d'un accent démarcatif sur la pénultième servant de limite de domaine pour l'association tonale.
sources.locator: theses.fr record 1992PA05H011, field "accessible": "non"; abstract (FR and EN)
sources.note: Only the abstract is reachable. It describes a comparative typology of ~30 East African Bantu prosodic systems ranging from fully tonal (Kikuyu) to purely demarcative penultimate stress (Swahili), with a diachronic hypothesis that the emergence of a penultimate demarcative accent drove the evolution of these systems. The abstract does not name Chaga or Machame, so whether Machame is among the ~30 sample languages, and how its tone/accent system is classified, cannot be read from any open source. Philippson's own later Kilimanjaro Bantu chapter (Philippson & Montlahuc 2003, held by the project…
